cells.tense: Right now you are the one who feels the shape of what has not settled yet and says it where others can hear.
cells.ask: Show one unfinished thing to one person who shares this work, before it is polished. Say what you hope it becomes, then let them respond.
cells.core:
You feel what is forming before it has a name, and you stay with it instead of forcing it into shape. The wide-open eyes are not naivety here — they are how words get found for something a group is still becoming. You bring the thing into the open early, and it comes back clearer than it started.

What carries this further is tending it past the interesting stage and keeping it warm once the shine wears off. So let one unfinished thing be seen by someone who keeps the same thing you keep. Let their answer change what you thought it was, and keep it open long enough to find out what it is.

cells.tense: You are living in a version of this that has not arrived yet, bracing for how it should land.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you keep proposing. Leave it unshared for three days. Write what happens instead — one line each evening.
cells.core:
You keep rehearsing how this should land before it has actually taken shape. There is a future where it comes across cleanly, and you are already living there, pitching toward a room that has not formed. Some of the fresh feeling starts to work like pressure to bring people along.

What the whole thing is for is quieter than that. Wait until the feeling is finished in you before you hand it out. The waiting costs you the buzz of being first, and it is worth paying. So pick one thing you keep proposing and sit with it. Better to grow slowly than to force something that needed more time.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door you already walked through, and the room on the other side has moved on without you.
cells.ask: Ask one person in this tradition what changed while you were away. Listen to the whole answer before you reply.
cells.core:
You know how to meet something new with open feeling, and it is still alive in you. In the good version of this, you walk straight into what is not settled, say what you sense, and let it change shape in the saying. But when you picture bringing it into a shared setting, the reach stops short — the thing stays in your head and does not come out.

What fills this back up is not pushing yourself to feel more. It is listening until you actually understand what people are carrying now. The room has moved on, and you can learn its shape from where they stand. Ask one person in this tradition what changed while you were gone, and let the answer land without a reply ready.
cells.sheetLine: You can feel what is new. You stopped bringing it anywhere.

cells.tense: You are already shaping what the people around you find meaningful, and you talk about it as if it were just happening.
cells.ask: Name one thing you changed in how this group does something, and say to one person there that it was your call.
cells.core:
You are already doing this. In the phrasing you reach for, in what you keep and what you quietly let go, the shared thing moves because of choices you make. When it is working, someone repeats a line you shaped and it sounds like theirs, which is the point. But you describe it as the thing having a life of its own — not as yours.

The choices are running; the claim on them is not. What settles it is practice, not more theory: check what you did against what you meant. So name one thing you changed in how this group does something, and say to one person there that it was your call. Nothing loud, just true.
cells.sheetLine: You are already shaping it. You call it the way things go.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the open, beginner's wonder is what feeds a shared tradition — the record only says vision flows from processed experience, not that a standing group wants or receives it. A reader could reasonably say the fresh feeling is in private, not in anything shared with anyone. The ask survives being wrong because showing one piece to a single person costs little and teaches something either way. The sentence serving the writer is the one about the room's appetite — I cut it.
